Last week you predicted a **number**: minutes of delivery time, grams of penguin.
The whole apparatus — a predictor, coefficients to interpret, a criterion to fit,
a baseline to beat, a held-out check — carries over to this week almost
unchanged. What changes is the outcome. This week it is a **label**: was the
delivery late, yes or no?

That is **logistic regression**, the topic of this week's lecture. By the end of
this lab you should be able to

  - explain why a straight line is the wrong tool for a probability;

  - fit a logistic regression model with `glm()`;

  - move between probabilities, odds and log-odds, and read $e^{b_1}$ as an
    odds ratio;

  - understand what maximum likelihood chooses, and why;

  - turn a predicted probability into a decision, and judge it with a confusion
    matrix;

  - extend the model to several predictors and to outcomes with more than two
    categories;

  - recognise the specific ways logistic models fail: separation, extrapolation
    and sampling variability.

As always, you are encouraged to experiment with the code. Change values,
change arguments, and check what happens.

# Part I: yes/no outcomes

## The same deliveries, a different question

We start from exactly the dataset you used last week: 37 deliveries, with the
distance travelled and the time taken.

```{r makedata}
deliveries <- data.frame(
  distance_km = c(1, 2, 2.8, 3, 3.2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7.7, 8, 8.3, 9,
                  10, 10, 10, 10, 11, 11.8, 12, 12.3, 13, 14, 15, 15, 15,
                  15, 16, 17, 17.8, 18, 18.3, 19, 20),
  time_min    = c(15, 13, 19, 18, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 20, 27, 27,
                  21, 22, 24, 26, 29, 32, 27, 33, 26, 27, 34, 34, 32, 34,
                  36, 37, 35, 40, 41, 37, 37, 42, 41))
```

The courier promises delivery **within 30 minutes**. Nothing about the data
changes; we simply ask a different question of it.

```{r mutate_deliveries}
deliveries <- deliveries %>%
  mutate(late = as.integer(time_min > 30))

table(deliveries$late)
```

```{r}
plot(time_min ~ distance_km, data = deliveries, las = 1,
     pch = 16, col = ifelse(deliveries$late == 1, "firebrick", "steelblue"),
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Time (min)")

abline(h = 30, col = "grey40", lwd = 2)
text(2, 31.5, "promise: 30 min", col = "grey40", cex = 0.8, adj = 0)
```

The outcome we now want to predict is the colour of the point, not its height.

```{r}
plot(jitter(late, amount = 0.02) ~ distance_km, data = deliveries, las = 1,
     pch = 16, col = ifelse(deliveries$late == 1, "firebrick", "steelblue"),
     ylim = c(-0.05, 1.05), yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Late?")
axis(2, at = c(0, 1), labels = c("0 (on time)", "1 (late)"), las = 1)
```

(The vertical wobble is `jitter()`, added only so that deliveries at the same
distance do not sit exactly on top of each other.)

## Why not just fit a straight line?

Nothing stops you running `lm()` on a 0/1 outcome. Let us see what happens.

```{r}
bad_fit <- lm(late ~ distance_km, data = deliveries)

coef(bad_fit)
```

```{r}

```

```{r}

     pch = 16, col = "firebrick", ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4),
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Late?")

abline(h = c(0, 1), col = "grey70")
abline(bad_fit, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
```

# Part II: the logistic model

## Fitting with `glm()`

Logistic regression puts the straight line on the **log-odds** scale,

$$\log\frac{p}{1-p}=b_0+b_1X,$$

which is equivalent to the S-shaped curve

$$\hat{p}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(b_0+b_1X)}}.$$

The function is `glm()` — *generalised* linear model — and the argument that
selects logistic regression is `family = binomial`.

```{r logitfit}
logit_fit <- glm(late ~ distance_km, data = deliveries, family = binomial)

coef(logit_fit)
```

Those coefficients live on the log-odds scale, so they are not directly
readable as minutes or probabilities. The easiest way to see what they say is
to draw the curve.

```{r}
grid <- data.frame(distance_km = seq(0, 21, length.out = 200))
grid$p <- predict(logit_fit, newdata = grid, type = "response")

plot(jitter(late, amount = 0.02) ~ distance_km, data = deliveries, las = 1,
     pch = 16, col = ifelse(deliveries$late == 1, "firebrick", "steelblue"),
     ylim = c(-0.05, 1.05),
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "P(late)")

lines(grid$distance_km, grid$p, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

Note the argument `type = "response"`. Without it, `predict()` returns
**log-odds**; with it, you get probabilities. This trips up almost everyone at
least once.

```{r}
predict(logit_fit, newdata = data.frame(distance_km = 12))                    # log-odds
predict(logit_fit, newdata = data.frame(distance_km = 12), type = "response") # probability
```

A coefficient on the log-odds scale becomes interpretable once you undo the
logarithm.

# Part III: fitting by maximum likelihood

Least squares does not work here: with a 0/1 outcome the residuals carry almost
no information about *how* wrong a prediction was. Logistic regression is fitted
instead by **maximum likelihood**: we choose the curve that makes the pattern of
lates and on-times we actually observed as probable as possible.

For a candidate pair $(b_0, b_1)$, each delivery contributes the probability
that curve assigned to what actually happened: $\hat{p}_i$ if it was late,
$1-\hat{p}_i$ if not. Multiplying those together gives the **likelihood**; in
practice we add their logarithms instead.

```{r loglik}
loglik <- function(b0, b1, data = deliveries){
  z <- b0 + b1 * data$distance_km
  p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
  # each delivery contributes log(p) if it was late, log(1 - p) if not
  return(sum(ifelse(data$late == 1, log(p), log(1 - p))))
}
```

```{r}
loglik(-13.2, 1.1)   # close to the fitted curve
loglik(-4.0, 0.35)   # a much flatter curve
loglik(0, 0)         # a curve that says 50-50 for every delivery
```

Higher is better: the fitted curve makes what we saw far more probable than
either alternative. R reports the same quantity for the fitted model:

```{r}
loglik(logit_fit)
```

# Part IV: from a probability to a decision

The model returns numbers like 0.11 and 0.78, but a dispatcher has to decide
whether to warn the customer. That needs a **threshold**.

```{r predlate}
p_hat <- predict(logit_fit, type = "response")

predicted_late <- as.integer(p_hat > 0.5)

table(predicted = predicted_late, actual = deliveries$late)
```

Read the table carefully: the diagonal holds the correct decisions, the
off-diagonal the two kinds of mistake — **false alarms** (warned, arrived on
time) and **misses** (not warned, arrived late).

```{r}
mean(predicted_late == deliveries$late)   # accuracy
```

Accuracy on its own means little. The lazy competitor ignores distance entirely
and always predicts "on time":

```{r}
mean(deliveries$late == 0)                # accuracy of always saying "on time"
```

Thirty-seven deliveries are enough to see the machinery work, but not enough to

```{r pengclean}

  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g), !is.na(flipper_length_mm),
```

```{r sexfit}
sex_fit <- glm(sex ~ body_mass_g, data = penguins_clean, family = binomial)

coef(sex_fit)
```

One detail matters enormously here. The outcome is a **factor**, and `glm()`
models the probability of its **second** level:

```{r}
levels(penguins_clean$sex)
```

So `sex_fit` predicts $P(\text{male})$, not $P(\text{female})$. Getting this
backwards is one of the most common errors in practice — always check
`levels()`.

```{r}
exp(100 * coef(sex_fit)[2])   # odds ratio for 100 g, a more natural step than 1 g
```

# Part VII: more than two categories

Not every categorical outcome has two levels. `species` has three, and nothing
about the logic changes: we choose a **reference category** and fit one equation
for each of the others. The function is `multinom()`, from the `nnet` package.

```{r spfit, results='hide'}
sp_fit <- multinom(species ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins_clean)
```

```{r}
round(coef(sp_fit), 3)
```

Each row is one equation, comparing that species with the reference — the first
level of the factor. The fitted probabilities always add to one across the three
species:

```{r}
head(round(predict(sp_fit, type = "probs"), 3))
```

```{r}
grid2 <- data.frame(flipper_length_mm = seq(170, 235, length.out = 200))
probs <- predict(sp_fit, newdata = grid2, type = "probs")

matplot(grid2$flipper_length_mm, probs, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("steelblue", "orange3", "firebrick"), las = 1,
        xlab = "Flipper length (mm)", ylab = "Predicted probability")

legend("left", bty = "n", legend = colnames(probs),
       col = c("steelblue", "orange3", "firebrick"), lwd = 2)
```

# Part VIII: how logistic models fail

## Separation

Logistic regression has a failure mode with no counterpart in linear
regression. If a predictor splits the two classes perfectly, there is no best
curve: a steeper one always fits better, and the fitting algorithm runs away.

This is a small-sample problem, and it is easy to trigger. Take just 16
penguins of two species:

```{r small}
two_species <- penguins_clean %>%
  filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Gentoo")) %>%
  mutate(is_gentoo = as.integer(species == "Gentoo"))

set.seed(1)
small <- two_species[sample(nrow(two_species), 16), ]

# in this sample, the flipper lengths of the two species do not overlap at all
range(small$flipper_length_mm[small$is_gentoo == 0])
range(small$flipper_length_mm[small$is_gentoo == 1])
```

## The fitted curve is an estimate too

```{r}
set.seed(2024)

slopes <- map_dbl(1:300, \(i){
  s <- penguins_clean %>% slice_sample(n = 100)
  coef(glm(sex ~ body_mass_g, data = s, family = binomial))[2]
})

hist(slopes, breaks = 25, col = "lightblue", las = 1,
     main = "Sampling distribution of the slope (n = 100)",
     xlab = "Estimated coefficient of body mass (log-odds per g)")

sd(slopes)
```

## Where this goes next

Both of the last two labs fitted a model, interpreted its coefficients,
measured its error against a baseline, and checked it on data it had not seen.
That sequence is not specific to lines or S-curves: it is what fitting any
predictive model looks like. What changes from one model to the next is the
shape of the curve and the criterion used to choose it — least squares here,
maximum likelihood there — and the vocabulary you now have for both.
